explanation: Shared libraries (also known as dynamic-link libraries or DLLs) are collections of compiled code and data that can be loaded into memory and linked to an executable program at runtime. This contrasts with static linking, where all necessary code is bundled directly into the executable. Dynamic linking allows multiple programs to share the same library code in memory, conserving system resources and enabling easier updates (only the shared library needs to be updated, not every program that uses it). The linker plays a crucial role in resolving references to functions and data within the shared library, ensuring that the program can correctly call library functions at runtime.  The process involves using a stub library to manage the calls and address resolution.
keywords: Shared Libraries, Dynamic Linking, DLL, Shared Object
